newsitem.title: LIBYA: Zaire says Libya offers to help it combat rebels.
newsitem.headline: Zaire says Libya offers to help it combat rebels.

text.p: Libya has offered to help Zaire retake territory from Rwandan-backed rebels whose offensive has threatened to break up the vast Central African country, official Radio Zaire said on Tuesday.

But opponents of Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo greeted with scepticism his formal order on Monday for the army, humiliated by the rebels at the end of 1996, to launch its long-promised counter-attack.
Radical opposition politicians doubted the beleagured army had the discipline or morale to fight. Other political rivals accused Kengo of throwing away any element of surprise.
Supporters of ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko, who is receiving cancer treatment in France, joined the fray, accusing Kengo of usurping presidential powers of declaring war.
Radio Zaire did not detail Tripoli's assistance offer but said this was the subject of talks between the visiting Libyan foreign minister and senior Zaire officials.
"The message of Libya's foreign minister is clear. Libya will assist Zaire in retaking the lost territories," the radio said, quoting the Libyan minister, Omar Mustafa al-Montasser.
"Libya is against foreign interference in Zaire's internal affairs and says that Zaire's territorial integrity must be restored," the radio said.
It said Egypt, whose special envoy was also visiting Kinshasa, shared the view.

Libya, isolated by U.N. sanctions for alleged support of terrorism, is among a handful of countries -- including France, China and Iran -- rumoured in Kinshasa to be helping Zaire prepare its counter-offensive.
Montasser arrived in Zaire from Cameroon on Monday, the day Kengo formally ordered the Zaire army to hit back at rebels.

"In the name of the government and in agreement with the president of the republic, I have today ordered our armed forces to conduct the war and recover regions currently under occupation and restore the authority of the state," Kengo said on state television.

"There are already plenty of problems within the army," radical opposition politician Joseph Olenghankoy told Reuters. "There is no morale. Nobody believes in (talk of) recovering the occupied territories."

Olenghakoy, parliamentary head of Zaire's powerful radical opposition, also criticised the government's widely publicised recruitment of mercenaries: "How can a Zairean soldier fight alongside mercenaries from various countries who are much better paid than he is."
Proponents of dialogue with rebel leader Laurent Kabila, who include some Mobutu supporters, accused Kengo of acting unconstitutionally.
"Only the president is empowered to declare war," said Bemba Saolona, a member of parliament close to Mobutu.

Bemba urged dialogue to end the conflict, which began when ethnic Tutsis rebelled last October after local authorities tried to expel them to Rwanda, their ancestral home. Mobutu has rejected dialogue.
Kengo's political associate Jean-Marie Rusimbuka came to the prime minister's support.

"One cannot negotiate from a position of weakness. We have to recover all our national territory before elections," he told Reuters. The war has cast doubts on elections expected by next May under a delayed transition to democracy.
